Ibn Kathir juge sa version d'Ibn 'Umar la plus authentique, tandis qu'al-Alusi recense plusieurs avis sans trancher. Ibn 'Uthaymin estime que le sens est l'audition utile. Ibn 'Ashur distingue trois catégories d'incroyants, chacune comparée à l'une de ces images. Al-Biqa'i et al-Alusi voient dans celui qui entend le croyant attentif et disposé à la foi, et y lisent une consolation pour le Prophète face à leur refus.

Ce verset rappelle que l'être humain traverse des étapes successives de faiblesse, de force, puis de nouveau de faiblesse accompagnée de cheveux blancs. Dieu l'a créé d'abord d'une goutte faible, puis lui a donné la force de la jeunesse, avant de le ramener à la faiblesse et à la vieillesse, selon Sa volonté, Sa science et Sa puissance. Les commentateurs s'accordent largement sur ce sens : la faiblesse initiale désigne la goutte de sperme ou l'enfance, la force désigne la jeunesse et la faiblesse finale la vieillesse. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir l'expliquent ainsi, et Ibn Kathir cite la transmission d'Ibn Umar qui a lu le verset avec la voyelle de la fatha puis a été corrigé par le Prophète pour la damma. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi rapportent que la lecture avec damma est plus forte, que la fatha est dialectale chez Tamim et la damma chez Quraysh. Al-Qurtubi et Abu Hayyan ajoutent que certains linguistes distinguent la faiblesse du corps (damma) et celle de l'esprit (fatha), ce que d'autres ne retiennent pas. Al-Razi et al-Nasafi estiment que la succession de ces états est la preuve la plus claire de la science et de la puissance du Créateur. Al-Mawardi et Qatada rapprochent les cheveux blancs du signe annonciateur de la mort. La suite du passage, où les criminels jurent n'être restés qu'une heure, est lue par al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir comme un mensonge, comme ils mentaient dans ce monde. Ibn 'Atiyya, lui, présente l'hypothèse qu'ils sous-estiment leur séjour terrestre face à l'au-delà, et Abu Hayyan évoque l'oubli ou le mensonge.

Ce verset annonce qu'au Jour de la Résurrection les criminels jureront qu'ils n'ont demeuré que peu de temps, qu'il s'agisse de la vie d'ici-bas ou du séjour dans les tombes. Les commentateurs expliquent qu'ils trouvent leur durée de vie très courte, soit par effroi devant ce qu'ils voient, soit parce qu'ils l'estiment brève au regard de ce qui les attend. Presque tous s'accordent à dire que ces criminels sont les polythéistes et les mécréants, et que leur serment est un mensonge, à l'image de celui qu'ils proféraient déjà en ce monde. Ibn Kathir voit dans ce serment une tentative d'échapper à la preuve, car ils n'ont pas été laissés le temps d'être avertis. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir rapportent que le mot « afaka » signifie être détourné de la vérité, et qu'ainsi ils sont détournés du vrai en ce monde comme dans l'au-delà.

Les avis divergent sur la durée visée. Qatada, al-Kalbi et Muqatil l'entendent de la vie terrestre, tandis que Muqatil et al-Kalbi l'entendent aussi du séjour dans les tombes, et que Yahya ibn Salam la place entre la mort et la résurrection. Al-Qurtubi relève qu'un hadith sur les quarante années entre les deux souffles ne suffit pas à trancher, et qu'il ne contredit pas le châtiment de la tombe. Al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir rattachent ensuite les versets suivants aux croyants instruits, qui répondent aux criminels que leur séjour était inscrit dans le Livre de Dieu jusqu'au jour de la Résurrection.

Al-Razi, al-Baydawi et Abu al-Su'ud rappellent par ailleurs que le mot « Sa'a », l'Heure, désigne l'Heure par excellence. Ils n'en tirent cependant aucune conclusion divergente sur le sens du verset lui-même.

Ce verset rapporte que ceux qui ont reçu la science et la foi, qui sont pour la plupart des commentateurs les anges, les prophètes et les croyants, répondent aux associateurs qui juraient n'être restés qu'une heure dans la vie d'ici-bas ou dans leurs tombes. Ils leur disent qu'ils ont demeuré dans le Livre de Dieu jusqu'au jour de la résurrection, et que c'est là le jour de la résurrection qu'ils niaient, mais qu'ils ne savaient pas qu'il aurait lieu. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi expliquent que le Livre désigne ce que Dieu a décrété dans Sa science antérieure. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi ajoutent qu'il peut désigner la Table gardée, le jugement divin ou le Coran lui-même. Qatada, Muqatil et al-Suddi estiment qu'il y a ici une inversion des termes, de sorte que ce sont ceux qui détiennent la science du Livre qui parlent. Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan jugent cette lecture éloignée de la construction du texte et n'y voient pas la nécessité.

Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que le « fa » de « fa-hadha yawmu al-ba'th » est la réponse à une condition sous-entendue, signifiant : si vous niez la résurrection, voici son jour. Ils voient dans ces paroles une réprimande et une confirmation de l'erreur des mécréants. Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Ashur précisent que les croyants répondent par l'argument même que les mécréants n'ont pas voulu accepter ici-bas. Al-Razi relie ces versets à la différence entre le coupable, qui juge le délai court, et le croyant, qui le juge long.

Le verset suivant ajoute, selon l'accord des commentateurs, que les injustes ne tirent aucun profit de leurs excuses ce jour-là et qu'on ne leur demande plus de rétablir la faveur divine par la repentance.

Ce verset annonce que, le jour de la Résurrection, les impies qui ont fait tort à eux-mêmes par leur mécréance ne tireront aucun profit de leurs excuses, et qu'on ne leur demandera pas de regagner la faveur de Dieu par le repentir et l'obéissance, comme cela leur était demandé ici-bas. Les commentateurs expliquent que les excuses désignent les justifications par lesquelles on cherche à écarter le châtiment, et que le verbe istiʿtiab signifie demander à être agréé, c'est-à-dire revenir à ce qui satisfait Dieu. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn ʿAtiyya rapportent que les mécréants jureront n'être restés dans le monde qu'une heure, et que les savants et les croyants leur répondront qu'ils sont demeurés dans le Livre de Dieu jusqu'au jour de la résurrection, mais qu'ils ne savaient pas. Al-Zamakhshari considère que le fa' de la phrase « voici le jour de la résurrection » répond à une condition sous-entendue : si vous niez la résurrection, voilà son jour. Sur le sens de l'istiʿtab, al-Nasafi et al-Baydawi retiennent qu'on ne leur dira pas de se repentir, tandis qu'al-Naqqash comprend qu'ils ne seront pas réprimandés pour leurs fautes, et que Yahya ibn Salam y voit un retour au monde pour croire. Sur l'identité de ceux qui ont reçu le savoir, al-Kalbi y voit les anges, Qatada et Ibn Jurayj les croyants, et d'autres les gens du Livre. Les lecteurs diffèrent entre le yā' et le tā' dans le verbe, sans que cela change le sens général, qui est que l'excuse ne sert plus à rien ce jour-là.

Ce verset affirme que Dieu a exposé aux hommes, dans le Coran, toutes sortes de paraboles et de descriptions frappantes, afin d'établir l'argument contre eux et de les appeler au monothéisme et à la vérité des messagers. Il ajoute que si les mécréants recevaient le moindre signe, ils diraient au Prophète et aux croyants qu'ils sont dans l'erreur et la falsification. Les commentateurs s'accordent à voir dans les « mécréants » des incrédules obstinés, et dans leur endurcissement la cause de leur refus. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir précisent que ce signe peut être une véritable miracle, comme le bâton de Moïse ou la fendue de la mer, ou même un verset du Coran, et qu'ils le rejetteraient quel qu'il soit, y voyant de la magie. Quant à la phrase « Ainsi Dieu scelle les cœurs de ceux qui ne savent pas », al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir l'expliquent comme un scellement qui empêche de comprendre les versets. Al-Zamakhshari, en revanche, interprète le sceau comme le retrait des grâces qui ouvrent le cœur à la vérité, position qu'il rattache à la doctrine mu'tazilite ; il note lui-même que la tradition sunnite affirme que Dieu crée ce scellement comme il crée le bien. Al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi parlent d'un savoir composé qui empêche de discerner le vrai. Le verset se conclut par l'ordre donné au Prophète de patienter, car la promesse de Dieu est vraie, et de ne pas se laisser ébranler par ceux qui ne croient pas à la résurrection. Al-Tabari rapporte à ce propos l'anecdote de l'homme kharijite qui interpella Ali pendant la prière de l'aube, auquel il répondit par ce même verset. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Ashur rapportent aussi une opinion selon laquelle ce verset serait abrogé, sans que cela soit tranché.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset vient après l'évocation de la façon dont les incrédules réagissent aux signes : Dieu indique que leur rejet de chaque signe découle de l'apposition d'un sceau sur leurs cœurs, c'est-à-dire d'une fermeture qui les empêche d'accepter la vérité et de comprendre les versets du Coran qui leur sont récités. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et al-Nasafi précisent qu'il s'agit des cœurs des ignorants, qui ne cherchent pas le savoir et persistent dans des croyances qu'ils se sont forgées. Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi et Ibn Kathir ajoutent que l'ignorance composée empêche de saisir la vérité et conduit à traiter de mensonge celui qui est dans le vrai. Al-Zamakhshari interprète le sceau comme le fait que Dieu retire les grâces qui ouvrent le cœur à la vérité, et il relève que, selon la doctrine sunnite, Dieu crée ce sceau et qu'il faut garder le verset dans son sens apparent, comme le note al-Alusi. Ibn 'Ashur y voit une disposition qui rend le cœur incapable de comprendre les questions religieuses, et il considère que ceux qui ne savent pas sont les incrédules eux-mêmes. Al-Razi remarque que celui qui ne sait pas maintenant a déjà été scellé auparavant. La plupart s'accordent à dire que le verset console le Prophète, et que le verset suivant l'exhorte à la patience, car la promesse de Dieu est vraie et que ceux qui ne croient pas ne doivent pas l'ébranler. Al-Sa'di et al-Biqa'i précisent que le savoir qui leur manque est le savoir utile qui guide vers la vérité. Certains rapportent aussi un épisode où un kharijite interpella Ali pendant la prière, mais les commentateurs n'en tirent pas de règle.

Ce verset ordonne au Prophète ﷺ de patienter face à l'hostilité des incroyants, car la promesse de Dieu est vraie et ne manquera pas. Il lui interdit aussi de se laisser ébranler par ceux qui n'ont pas de certitude. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi comprennent cette promesse comme le secours du Prophète et l'établissement de ses compagnons sur terre, tandis qu'al-Mawardi y voit aussi la vengeance contre les ennemis, et qu'al-Sam'ani y voit la promesse de la Résurrection. Quant au verbe « istakhaffa », les commentateurs proposent des sens voisins : ne pas te presser, ne pas t'ébranler, ne pas t'entraîner dans l'égarement. Les « sans certitude » sont, pour la plupart, ceux qui nient la résurrection et le jugement ; Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi les décrivent comme des sceptiques égarés, et Abu Hayyan comme des gens qui ne croient pas à la victoire promise. Plusieurs commentateurs, dont al-Tha'alibi, rapportent un récit selon lequel un Kharijite, pendant la prière de l'aube, adressa à Ali une menace tirée d'un autre verset, et Ali lui répondit par ce même verset au cours de la prière. Zamakhshari rapporte aussi une lecture minoritaire, « yastahiqqanaka », et Ibn al-Qayyim relie la fermeté au degré de patience et de certitude. Al-Shinqiti précise que ce discours, bien qu'adressé au Prophète, vise en réalité à instruire sa communauté, car il est préservé de l'incroyance.
en:
The commentators explain that this opening passage reports the defeat of the Byzantines (al-Rum) by the Persians in the nearest land, and their future victory within a few years (bid‘ sinin), that the command belongs to God before and after, and that the believers will rejoice in God's help on that day. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ‘Atiyya and others agree that the Byzantines were People of the Book while the Persians were fire-worshippers or pagans, which is why the Muslims wished for the Byzantines' victory and the polytheists for the Persians'. When the defeat came, the Meccan idolaters rejoiced and taunted the Muslims, and these verses were revealed to announce the reversal.

Opinions differ on the location of the battle: Ibn ‘Abbas says the edge of Syria, Mujahid the Jazira, Muqatil Jordan and Palestine, ‘Ikrima Adhri‘at. As to the period, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that bid‘ means three to nine years, while some lexicographers say three to ten. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that Abu Bakr wagered with Ubayy ibn Khalaf on this prediction, and the Prophet ﷺ advised him to raise the stakes and extend the term. The Byzantines defeated the Persians in the seventh year, according to some at Badr, according to others at Hudaybiyya.

As for the believers' joy, most exegetes read it as joy that the People of the Book had defeated the Magians, and also as joy in the Muslims' victory over the polytheists at Badr; others see it as confirmation that the prophecy was true. Ibn ‘Atiyya suggests it can be explained by the natural preference for the defeat of the lesser enemy.

In sum, this is a true prophetic announcement: sovereignty belongs to God, the believers rejoice in His help, and He grants victory to whom He wills, for He is the Mighty, the Merciful.

This passage of Surah Ar-Rum announces that the Romans, a people of the Book, were defeated by the Persians in the part of the Levant nearest to Persia, but that they will prevail over them within a few years, a "bid'" that the linguists place between three and nine years. The commentators agree that the first defeat went to the Persians, that the Romans' victory will follow, and that all affairs belong to God both before and after. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others report that the verses were revealed when the Meccan polytheists rejoiced at the Persian success, since they favoured the Magians, idol-worshippers like themselves, while the Muslims wished for a Roman victory because the Romans were People of the Book. These authors also recount the wager between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf about the timing of the Roman victory, and note that the Prophet ﷺ told Abu Bakr to raise the stakes and extend the term, since the bid' lies between three and nine years. The reports differ on when the victory came: Ibn Abbas, Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri say it was on the day of Badr, while Ikrima, al-Zuhri and Qatada place it at Hudaybiyya, and Ibn Kathir leans towards about seven years later. As for "the nearest land", Mujahid identifies it as al-Jazira, Ibn Abbas as the edge of Syria, al-Suddi as Jordan and Palestine, and Ikrima as Adhri'at. Ibn Atiyya judges the reading with an initial ghayn to be the more sound, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the verse as proof of prophecy, since it foretells the future. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the believers' joy either as confirmation of the divine word, or because the Romans are People of the Book, or as a sign of their own coming victory over the polytheists. Modern commentators such as Ibn Ashur, al-Sha'rawi and Sayyid Qutb preserve the same meaning while stressing the prophetic dimension of the verse.

These opening verses of Surah Ar-Rum report that the Byzantines were defeated by the Persians in the nearest part of the land to Persia, and promise that they will defeat them in return within a few years. The commentators explain that 'bid' means a number between three and nine, that the command belongs to God both before and after these reversals, and that the believers will rejoice in God's help when the Byzantines prevail. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place this land at the edge of Syria, near Adhri'at and Busra. Mujahid locates it in al-Jazira, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi place it in Jordan and Palestine, and al-Zamakhshari relates it to the land of the Arabs. All agree that the Byzantines were People of the Book, that the Muslims wished them victory, and that the pagans of Mecca rejoiced at the Persian triumph. The accounts differ on when the second victory came: most say it was in the seventh year, but Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Muqatil link it to Badr, and others to Hudaybiyya. Ibn Kathir considers some of these chains strange. The exegetes see the passage as a sign of prophethood, since it reports something unseen. They also debate the wager between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf: Abu Hanifa used it to justify certain void contracts in enemy territory, while the majority held that it predated the prohibition of gambling.

The commentators explain that the Romans, defeated by the Persians in the land nearest to them, would prevail again within a few years, which most place between three and nine, some up to ten. They stress that the command belongs to God both before and after the defeat, and that the believers will rejoice in God's victory on that day. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the battle site is identified by some as Adhri'at and Busra, by others as al-Jazira, and by others as Jordan and Palestine. These authors also relate that Abu Bakr wagered with Ubayy ibn Khalaf on this term, and the Prophet advised him to raise the stakes and extend the deadline. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the wager took place before gambling was forbidden, while al-Alusi questions how the gain could be called unlawful gain. Ibn 'Atiyya explains the believers' joy by the Romans being People of the Book, unlike the idolatrous Persians, and al-Razi adds that their joy also related to the victory over the polytheists at Badr. Most see the verses as a proof of prophethood, since they announce an unseen event that came to pass. They conclude that God's promise never fails, yet most people do not know this, knowing only the outward side of worldly life and remaining heedless of the Hereafter.

This verse, the fifth of Surat al-Rum, belongs to the prophecy that the Byzantines would defeat the Persians after being defeated by them. It states that victory belongs to God, who grants it to whom He wills among His servants; He is the Mighty, whom nothing can overpower, and the Merciful toward His friends. The commentators agree that the passage refers to a battle between Romans and Persians on the Syrian frontier and to a Roman victory within a span of a few years, between three and nine, or ten years. The believers rejoiced because the Romans were People of the Book. Al-Tabari reports that the phrase 'by the victory of God' was read as God's victory granted to the People of the Book over the Magians, while Ibn Kathir and al-Razi see in the verse a proof of prophethood, since it announces something unseen. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also note that God's victory may mean the manifestation of the believers' truthfulness against the polytheists, or that God set the wrongdoers against one another until they destroyed each other. The commentators differ on the exact place of the battle: al-Mujahid places it in al-Jazira, Muqatil in Jordan and Palestine, and Ikrima in Adhruat. The wager between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf about the timing of the victory is related by most exegetes, with varied details on the stakes and the duration, and none of them decides between these accounts. The commentators all understand the closing phrase, 'God's is the command before and after', as affirming that every victory and defeat comes by His decree.

The commentators explain that this verse confirms the earlier promise that the Byzantines (al-Rum), after being defeated by the Persians in the nearest land, would overcome them again. This divine promise cannot be broken. According to most exegetes, such as Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, "most people" first refers to the disbelievers of Mecca, who did not grasp the truth of this promise. Several commentators link the event to the Byzantine victory over the Persians, which some place at the battle of Badr and others at Hudaybiyya.

Scholars agree that God does not break His word, since He is free of lying and incapacity. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi regard the phrase "God does not fail His promise" as an explanation of "the promise of God" and a way of affirming its certainty. Abu Hayyan notes that the verb "to know" here is used as if intransitive, as though these people had no real knowledge at all.

The second part of the verse, "they know only an outward appearance of the life of this world", is explained by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan as knowledge of livelihood, farming, trade and crafts. Sa'id ibn Jubayr understood it as what the devils reported about worldly affairs. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur stress that the verse blames heedlessness of the Hereafter rather than worldly knowledge in itself. Ibn Ashur adds that the repetition of the pronoun serves to emphasise this heedlessness.

Ibn Uthaymin observes that the passage shows that true knowledge is knowledge of God, His names and attributes, while knowledge of this world remains limited and superficial.

The commentators explain that this verse (al-Rum, 7) describes the state of the unbelieving Meccans and those like them: they know the outward appearance of the worldly life, meaning what their senses grasp of their livelihoods, such as farming, trade, crafts, building and their timing. Al-Hasan al-Basri reports that one of them can weigh a coin with the tip of his fingernail yet does not know how to pray. Concerning the Hereafter they are heedless: it does not come to their minds, they do not reflect on it and they do not act for it. The exegetes place the verse after God's promise that the Romans would defeat the Persians, and most see in it a rebuke and reproach rather than a condemnation of worldly knowledge as such. Al-Tabari also cites Ibn Jubayr's view that the apparent knowledge is what the devils snatch of worldly news when they eavesdrop on the heavens. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take the word apparent to mean what is perceptible to the senses. Ibn Juzayy holds that it means knowledge of worldly affairs and their benefits, since the verse goes on to describe them as heedless of the Hereafter. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi distinguish the outward side of this world, its pleasures, from its inward side, which is that it leads to the Hereafter. Ibn 'Uthaymin considers the verse to cover anyone without faith, while others restrict it to the disbelievers. The commentators present these views side by side without weighing one against another.

This verse calls people to reflect on themselves and on the universe. It shows that the creation of the heavens, the earth and what lies between them is not in vain but based on truth and justice, and that it has a fixed term, which Ibn 'Abbas and most commentators identify as the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that reflecting on one's own existence, from nothingness through the stages of life to death, shows that the One who created can also resurrect. Al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi note that the word 'haqq' may mean justice, wisdom, or the establishment of truth. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the particle 'bi' to indicate accompaniment: creation is joined to wisdom. Opinions differ on 'in their own selves': al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya allow that it denotes the place of reflection or its object, while Ibn 'Ashur sees in it evidence drawn from the nature of beings themselves. Many commentators, such as al-Qurtubi, stress that the call concerns the creation of the heavens and earth, and that reflecting on oneself is a route to it. As for the addressees, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir link them to the Quraysh, whereas al-Sa'di widens the address to all who deny the resurrection. The 'meeting with their Lord' is generally understood as resurrection and judgment. All agree that the verse establishes resurrection through reason, and that many people reject it despite clear proofs. Commentators link the following verse to traveling the earth to consider the fate of earlier peoples, who were stronger and more prosperous, yet whose strength did not save them when they denied their messengers; God did not wrong them, for they wronged themselves.

This verse calls the deniers to travel through the earth and reflect on the fate of the peoples who came before them. Those peoples were stronger than them and had cultivated and built the land more extensively, yet when they denied their messengers who brought clear proofs, God destroyed them. The commentators note that God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves through disbelief, denial and disobedience.

The commentators agree that "those before them" refers to the destroyed nations such as ʿAd and Thamud, and that the verse rebukes and warns the people of Mecca, who passed by their ruins on their journeys. They also agree that the negation of injustice in God shows His perfect justice. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada explained as-sou'a as the Fire or punishment, al-Suddi as Hell, and al-Hasan as punishment in this world and the next.

Scholars differ on the meaning of stirring up the earth and cultivating it. Mujahid, al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir took it to mean ploughing and tilling for crops, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi included drawing out water and extracting minerals. Al-Zamakhshari held that the comparison with the Meccans is meant to mock their weakness in worldly matters, since they lived in a valley without crops. Ibn 'Uthaymin saw ploughing as a source of strength and understood cultivation to include building and trade.

As for the word "that" in "because they denied", al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj read it as giving the cause, namely their denial of God's signs and their mockery of them. Ibn Kathir notes that as-sou'a may be the object of "they did wrong" or the predicate of "was". The commentators agree that the passage teaches the reader to reflect on history.

This verse in Surah al-Rum says that the outcome for those who did evil was the worst of ends, al-su'a, meaning the most dreadful punishment. Most commentators understand the evil deed to be disbelief and the denial of God's signs. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada explain al-su'a as the Fire, and al-Tabari reports their view that those who associated partners with God will be cast into it. Al-Suddi and others take al-Su'a to be a name of Hell, just as al-Husna is a name of Paradise, while al-Hasan al-Basri holds that it means punishment both in this world and the next.

Regarding the signs they denied and mocked, al-Kalbi identifies them with the Qur'an and the Prophet, Muqatil with the punishment that would befall them, and al-Dahhak with the miracles of the messengers. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi likewise stress that hostility to the truth brought about this end.

The main disagreements concern grammar. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read 'aqibatu in the nominative as the subject of kana, whereas 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'aqibata in the accusative as a fronted predicate. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan propose that 'an kadhdhabu' is a cause, a substitute or an apposition, or that 'an' is explanatory; Abu Hayyan finds the last reading forced. Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti understand al-su'a as the greatest of evils. Ibn 'Ashur adds that 'thumma' here marks a rise in rank, since this end exceeds worldly punishment, and that the verse warns the pagans of Mecca.

This verse states that Allah alone originates creation, then brings it back again, and that finally you will be returned to Him. Al-Tabari explains that He creates alone, without partner or helper, from nothing, and that after annihilation He recreates creatures anew, just as He first made them. Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion that whoever can begin creation can also restore it, and that the return to Him takes place on the Day of Resurrection, when each doer is repaid for his deeds. The verse thus establishes resurrection by an argument from divine power: the One who created at first cannot be prevented from creating again.

The commentators agree on the general meaning: the first creation and the resurrection belong to the same power, and the return to God is for reckoning and recompense. Al-Razi notes that this argument answers the disbelievers, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a proof the polytheists cannot deny, since they already acknowledge that Allah alone creates. Ibn 'Uthaymin observes that the word "al-khalq" functions as a verbal noun meaning "the created beings," which explains why the pronoun is singular in "yu'iduhu" yet plural in "turji'un."

The differences concern mainly the reading and the form of the verb. Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read "yurji'un" in the third person, while most readers read "turja'un" in the second person. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain this shift from the third person to direct address as a means of intensifying the warning. Al-Zamakhshari simply notes that the return is to His reward and His punishment. These variations do not change the overall meaning of the verse.

God states that He originates creation, then brings it back, and that to Him you will be returned for judgment. On the verse "On the day the Hour arises, the criminals will be struck dumb," the commentators describe the guilty as despairing of all good and falling silent, bewildered and without any argument. Mujahid renders the verb as "being exposed," Ibn 'Abbas as "despairing," Qatada and al-Kalbi as "losing hope of all good," and al-Farra' as "their speech and proof cut off." Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba also give the senses of remorse, distress and confusion, citing a line of al-'Ajjaj. Al-Tabari combines distress, remorse and despair, while Ibn Zayd understands the one who is struck dumb to be one on whom calamity has fallen.

The commentators agree that these criminals, the polytheists, will find no intercessors among the powers they worshipped, and that they will even disown them. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, followed by others, explain that the separation mentioned next is the distinguishing of the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire, and that this parting is final, as Qatada says. As for the meadow in which the believers will be made glad, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas takes it as being honoured, Mujahid and Qatada as enjoying blessings, al-Sudi as rejoicing, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir as delighting in music.

Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also discuss the readings of the verb "yublisu," with the lam vowelled either with kasra or fatha, the latter attributed to 'Ali and al-Sulami. The commentators draw no legal ruling from this passage; they focus on explaining its meaning and the scene it depicts.

This passage describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection: when the Hour arrives, the criminals, meaning the polytheists, will be overwhelmed and fall silent, finding no intercessor among the deities they worshipped besides God, and those deities will disown them. Commentators give the verb yublisu related meanings: disgrace, grief, remorse, bewilderment, despair of any outlet, or silence before a lost argument. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite explanations from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, while al-Mawardi lists six. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the partners to be idols, whereas Muqatil identifies them as angels and al-Alusi also mentions devils or their leaders. All agree that people are then divided into two groups: those of Paradise, who will be delighted and joyful, and those of the Fire, who will be brought forcibly into punishment and remain there. Ibn Abbas takes tahbarun to mean being honoured, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean enjoying blessings, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir takes it as enjoying music. Ibn Ashur and Abu Hayyan note the rhetorical force of the indefinite rawda and the definite al-adhab. The passage closes with the call to glorify God at the times of prayer, following Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, which Ibn Kathir extends to the five daily prayers.

This verse describes the Day when the Hour is established and people separate into two groups: believers and disbelievers. The commentators explain that this separation takes place after the reckoning, with some going to Paradise and others to the Fire. The pronoun 'they will be separated' refers to both believers and disbelievers, as held by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi. Qatada adds that it is a final separation: the one group raised to the highest places, the other lowered to the lowest. Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as a separation of abodes, judgments and rewards, while al-Hasan describes it as a distinction between Muslims in 'Illiyyin and disbelievers in the lowest depths. The next verse states that those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in a meadow where they are made joyful and blessed. Ibn 'Abbas explains 'yuhbarun' as honoured, Mujahid and Qatada as given bounties, and al-Suddi as rejoicing. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and al-Awza'i take it to mean listening to songs and music in Paradise, and reports are cited for this view. Ibn Kathir holds that the word encompasses all these meanings. As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, they will be brought forth to the punishment, never absent from it and never lightened; al-Baghawi reads 'mahdarun' as gathered, al-Qurtubi as tormented. Al-Razi notes that the verse begins with the believers even though the context concerns the criminals, because the reward reaches the believer before the punishment reaches the disbeliever, making it more painful for the latter. Ibn al-Qayyim discusses at length the audition of Paradise, distinguishing what is granted in the Hereafter from what is permitted in this world.

This verse, set in the scene of the Day of Resurrection, describes the fate of those who believed and did righteous deeds: they will be in a rawda, a flourishing garden, and they will be made joyful. The commentators explain that a rawda is land full of plants and water, which the Arabs considered the most beautiful of places, and that its indefinite form expresses its grandeur and refers to Paradise. On the meaning of yuhbarun, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as being honoured, Mujahid and Qatada as being blessed with abundance, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Suddi as being delighted, and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and al-Awza'i as hearing singing in Paradise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that these meanings all go back to a single idea of joy and bounty, with the music included. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi, cite hadiths and reports about the music of the people of Paradise. Ibn al-Qayyim discusses whether this verse can be used to justify listening to music in this world, showing that the question is contested among scholars. Set against this is the fate of the disbelievers, who will be present in punishment without being absent from it or relieved, as al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to those who disbelieved, denied God's messengers and rejected the Resurrection: they are "muhdarun", meaning brought forth and kept in punishment, never absent from it and never relieved. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir keep this sense, while al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi render it as "remaining", "entering" or "never leaving". Al-Sam'ani and al-Zamakhshari read it as "tormented". The verse contrasts with the one before it, which describes believers who do good deeds and are joyfully settled in a garden. Ibn Abbas takes the word "yuhbarun" to mean "honoured", Mujahid and Qatada "blessed", and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir "hearing singing in Paradise". Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari place these meanings together as forms of delight. The following verses command glorifying God in the evening and the morning. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take this to mean the five daily prayers, while other exegetes understand it as a general glorification. Ibn Ashur notes that "rawda" denotes a green, watered place, here Paradise. The commentators agree on the central point: the final separation between believers and disbelievers, with lasting joy for the one and lasting punishment for the other.

This verse tells believers to glorify God and declare Him free of all imperfection at particular times of the day: when evening falls, when morning comes, in the late afternoon, and at midday. Most commentators read it as a reference to the obligatory prayers. Ibn Abbas, asked by Nafi ibn al-Azraq whether the five prayers appear in the Quran, recited this verse. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Mujahid and Qatada take it as naming the five prayers: maghrib and isha for "when you enter the evening", fajr for "when you enter the morning", asr for "the late afternoon", and dhuhr for "when you enter midday". Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi report the same reading, attributing it to Ibn Abbas and others.

On the meaning of tasbih, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir explain it as declaring God free of every defect and praising Him for the blessings renewed at these times. Al-Razi holds that the fullest glorification combines heart, tongue and limbs, with prayer as its most excellent form, and he sees in it a way of filling time with continual praise. Some scholars treat tasbih as a verbal noun standing in place of an imperative. The clause "to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth" is generally taken as a parenthesis between the times, meaning that all who can discern must praise God.

Al-Hasan held that the surah is Medinan, since he said the five prayers were prescribed in Medina, whereas most scholars maintain they were prescribed in Mecca. Several hadiths on the merit of reciting this verse in the morning and evening are cited; Ibn Kathir judged some of their chains weak, while al-Shawkani accepted some of them for the general merit of tasbih.

This verse calls believers to glorify God and praise Him at set times of the day, the evening, the morning, the late afternoon and midday, and states that praise belongs to Him alone in the heavens and on earth. Most commentators see in these times an allusion to the five daily prayers. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Qatada and Ibn Zayd relate them to maghrib and isha, fajr, asr and dhuhr respectively. Al-Hasan al-Basri therefore held that the verse was revealed in Medina, since he believed the five prayers were made obligatory there, whereas most scholars hold that they were prescribed in Mecca. Al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani understand the glorification as prayer itself and the praise as thanks to God. Al-Razi reads the glorification as a declaration of God's transcendence that includes belief in the heart, remembrance on the tongue and good deeds, with prayer being its best form. Al-Mawardi explains that glorification is linked to the night and praise to the day, because during the day a person lives through circumstances that call for thanks. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi treat the clause « and to Him belongs praise » as a parenthesis between the time expressions, meaning that all discerning beings should praise God. On the phrase about praise in the heavens and the earth, Ibn 'Abbas says their inhabitants praise Him and pray to Him. Ibn Kathir cites several narrations on the merit of reciting these words morning and evening without ruling between the chains. Most commentators explain that « He brings the living out of the dead » refers to a human from a drop of semen or a bird from an egg, and that the revival of dead land by plants serves as a proof of resurrection.

The commentators explain that the verse means that God brings the living out of the dead, like a human from a drop of semen or a bird from an egg, and brings the dead out of the living, like the drop or the egg. He also revives the earth with plants after it has dried up, and in the same way you will be brought forth from your graves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi largely agree on this plain, concrete sense, and see the renewal of the earth as a sign of God's power over the resurrection, since restoring creation is as easy for Him as originating it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also report that the living and the dead may denote the believer and the disbeliever, an opinion attributed to al-Hasan and 'Umar. Ibn Kathir treats the verse as one of many that pair opposites to show the completeness of God's power. Ibn 'Atiyya separates the literal sense, the semen and the egg, from the figurative sense, the sprouting of plants from the earth and of grain from the plant. Al-Razi reports that some understand it as the waking person coming out of sleep and the reverse, as an illustration. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as an indirect reply to the polytheists and a hint at the guidance of those who came from unbelief. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir observe that the verse confirms the validity of analogical reasoning and that the Qur'an uses the revived earth to establish belief in resurrection. Many link the verse to the preceding command to glorify God at the hours of prayer, which some identify with the five daily prayers. Readers differ on whether the taa in tukhrajuna is vowelled as passive or active, and on the reading of al-mayyit, without any real change in the main meaning.

The commentators explain that this verse is one of God's signs showing His power and the reality of resurrection. God created the origin of mankind, Adam, from earth, and then his descendants became human beings spread across the earth. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir understand the creation from earth to refer to the creation of their father Adam, and the word 'human beings' to refer to his descendants. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take the address to include all people, since each person comes from earth through food from plants that becomes semen. Al-Razi lists this view alongside other interpretations. All agree that 'spreading out' means moving about, travelling and dispersing across the earth to seek a livelihood.

The following verses, which mention spouses, affection and mercy, have received different readings. Qatada and others report that Eve was created from Adam's rib, whereas al-Kalbi and Ali ibn Isa understand that God made spouses of the same kind as humans. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi stress that sharing the same kind is the basis of attachment. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ikrima take affection to mean marital intimacy and mercy to mean children, al-Sudi understands love and compassion, and others see mutual affection between the spouses.

As for recitation, Hafs reads 'lil-'alimin' with a kasra, while the majority reads it with a fatha; al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that the kasra reading restricts the benefit of the sign to people of knowledge.

The commentators explain that this verse is among God's signs that reveal His power and wisdom: He created for you, from your own kind, spouses so that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the spouses refer mainly to Hawwa, created from Adam's rib, while Ali ibn Isa, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take them to mean spouses in general, created of the same human kind. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan accept both meanings, leaning toward the sense of kind because it fits the phrase "that you may find rest in them."

On affection and mercy the views differ. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrima and others understand them as sexual union and offspring. Al-Sudd and Ibn Abbas understand them as love and compassion, al-Kalbi distinguishes love for the elder from tenderness toward the young, and Muqatil speaks of mutual compassion between the spouses. Some say affection is for the young wife and mercy for the older one.

The commentators agree that the verse calls for reflection and that the signs it mentions all point to God's power, knowledge and wisdom and to the truth of resurrection. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir take reflection to mean contemplating God's greatness, while al-Mahayimi and al-Qasimi take it to mean examining the wonders of His works, which rest on profound wisdom.

Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb show that the verse sets out the purpose of marriage, in which tranquillity, affection and mercy are its fruits. Most commentators draw no legal rulings from this passage.

The commentators explain that this verse counts among the signs of God that show His power and wisdom: the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of tongues and colours among people. These are proofs of His oneness and of His ability to resurrect the dead. Al-Tabari notes that the One who created the heavens and the earth cannot be incapable of bringing people back after death. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'tongues': al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi take it as the variety of languages, Arabic and foreign, while al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi also understand it as the variety of vocal tones, so that two brothers' voices are not alike. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it to mean the varieties of speech and pronunciation. As for colours, most understand white, black and red, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi include the shape and features of the body. All agree that this diversity is wise, since it makes recognition and distinction possible, and without it people's affairs would be disrupted. Hafs reads 'lil-'alimin' with a kasra, meaning those who have knowledge, whereas the majority reading with a fatha means all creatures. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi connect this verse with the surrounding verses on sleep, seeking provision, lightning and rain, which together indicate God's oneness and the resurrection. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di stress that the diversity of peoples is a clear sign of divine design.

This verse from Surah Ar-Rum lists among God's signs the sleep people take by night and by day, and their pursuit of His bounty, meaning the work by which they earn their living. The commentators differ on how the words are arranged. Some read it as sleep at night and striving by day. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take the view that sleep and striving both fall in the two periods, since the Qur'an's own usage supports this most. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the reversal of order to be weak, and al-Baydawi and al-Alusi see the arrangement as a rhetorical device that binds the two times together. Al-Razi notes that the verse ends with a call to listen carefully, because these matters are not always obvious and call for someone who guides the mind to them. Many scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, describe sleep as rest for the body and striving as the seeking of provision. Ibn 'Ashur sees sleep as resembling death and waking as resembling resurrection, so the verse is an argument for the afterlife. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the word for evening covers the early part of the night, and al-Sha'rawi reflects on how the mystery of sleep shows God's power.

The commentators explain that this verse is among the signs of God that demonstrate His power and knowledge. He shows you lightning, which arouses fear of thunderbolts or of rain harmful to the traveller, and hope for the beneficial rain for the resident. Then He sends down water from the sky that brings the earth back to life after its death. They agree that the verse is evidence of God's power to resurrect the dead and of the necessity of affirming His oneness, and that it is a sign for people who use their reason. Qatada says the fear is for the traveller and the hope for the one who stays put, while al-Dahhak understands the fear as fear of lightning and the hope as hope for rain. Yahya ibn Sallam takes the fear to be of cold that destroys the crops and the hope of rain that revives them. Ibn Bahr adds the fear that the lightning may be dry without rain, and the hope that it will bring rain. Al-Razi notes the benefit of seeing lightning before rain, since it warns people to prepare, and observes that the Bedouins do not know green lands unless they have seen the flashes. Grammarians differ over the omitted particle "an" after "yurikum": the Basran and Kufan schools assume it, while others treat the verb as a verbal noun. Most see the fear and hope as objects of purpose, though their subject differs from that of the main verb, which leads some to supply a complement or to read them as circumstantial states. Ibn Kathir holds that lightning arouses fear of violent rains and hope for needed rain, and that the revival of the dead earth illustrates resurrection. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the lightning electrical forces in the clouds and a divine wisdom in its arousing both fear and hope. All therefore agree that the verse is proof of divine power from which thinking people benefit, while the details of fear, hope and grammar remain debated.

The commentators explain that this verse is among the signs of God's power: the heavens and the earth stand firm by His command, that is by His word or His will, without visible pillars, which shows His complete power. The verse then announces the resurrection. When God calls mankind with a single summons from the earth, through the blast of Israfil on the trumpet, people will come out of their graves alive and hastening, without any delay. Several exegetes liken this swiftness to a subject who answers at once the call of an obeyed master.

Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, agree that the summons from the earth is the call to rise from the graves at the resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas says it means from the graves. Al-Mawardi reports, besides this, the view that the bringing out is by something equivalent to a command of "Be, and it is", and Qatada holds that the call comes from heaven. Al-Sam'ani reports that some said the call comes from a rock in Jerusalem, or from the sky, and that it is the call of Israfil. Ibn 'Atiyya allows that "from the earth" may qualify the call or describe the state of those called.

Readers differ on the vowelling of the verb "takhrujūn". Al-Qurtubi finds the reading with a fatha more suitable here, since going out is an act performed by people. According to most exegetes, the second "idhā" signals suddenness and takes the place of the particle "fa" in the conditional answer. The meaning retained by Ibn Kathir and most others is that the resurrection will happen all at once, without delay.

This verse states that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, in creation, ownership and governance, and that all of it submits to Him. The commentators differ on the meaning of qanitun. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as obedience, al-Kalbi limits it to those among them who obey, Qatada and Ikrima take it as acknowledging servitude, al-Hasan as standing witness to God's oneness, Ibn Jubayr as sincerity, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas as standing on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari prefers obedience to God's sovereign disposal over life, death and resurrection, even though some disobey in what they choose to do; Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as submission to God's acts upon them. The verse continues with the beginning and return of creation. Mujahid, Ikrima and Abu al-'Aliya hold that restoring creation is easier than originating it, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym read the phrase as meaning simply 'easy'. Al-Hasan argues that resurrection is simpler for the creatures, who rise at one call. Ibn 'Atiyya finds it more likely that the pronoun refers to God, supported by the next clause, 'His is the highest similitude', which Qatada explains as there being no god but Him and Ibn 'Abbas as nothing being like Him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that the placement of the complement shifts the emphasis in comparison with another verse.

The commentators explain that God is the One who originates creation and then brings it back after death for the resurrection, and that this return is "easier" for Him as humans conceive it, since repeating something is generally simpler than originating it, which brings the matter closer to human understanding. They differ on the meaning of "easier": Ibn Abbas, al-Rabi ibn Khuthaym, al-Hasan and Qatada take it as "effortless" (hayyin), since nothing is hard for God, citing Arabic usages where the af'al form means the fa'il form. Mujahid, Ikrima and one report from Ibn Abbas take it literally as a comparative: the resurrection is simpler in the eyes of people. Some say the pronoun "Him" refers to creation, which will be restored more easily, arising at a single cry rather than through successive stages from drop to embryo.

As for "His is the highest example", Ibn Abbas understands it as "nothing is like Him", Qatada and Mujahid as the testimony that there is no god but God, and others as the highest attribute of power and wisdom. The verse closes with "the Mighty, the Wise", the first describing His dominion and ability to punish, the second His governance and the perfection of His acts.

Other tafsirs raise here the question of qunut: Ibn Abbas renders it as obedience in life, death and resurrection, others as acknowledging servitude, and others as standing before God on the Day of Judgment. They also differ on the scope of "all are obedient to Him", some restricting it to the obedient believers. The example that follows, that of a slave who does not share his master's wealth, serves to show the absurdity of associating partners with God.

In this verse God offers an example drawn from people's own circumstances: would any of you accept that a slave you own should share with you, as an equal, the wealth God has given you, so that you fear he might act on his own against your wishes, as you fear a free partner? If you would not accept this for yourselves, how can you assign to God partners from among his servants? The commentators agree that this example, which reason can grasp, refutes polytheism. They differ over the meaning of the fear. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Mijlaz take it as fear that the slave would inherit or share in one's property; al-Tabari favours sharing over inheritance, while Yahya ibn Sallam and others read it as fear of blame. On the occasion of revelation, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil report that the polytheists used to recite the talbiyah: 'No partner for You, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns.' Al-Suddi reports that they did not pass on inheritance to their freed slaves. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the interrogative carries the sense of negation, that the first 'min' marks the starting point, the second indicates partial reference, and the third reinforces the negation. The commentators conclude that God explains His signs through such comparisons for people who reflect. As for those who follow their desires without knowledge, no one can guide those whom God has led astray, and they have no helpers.

This verse states that the polytheists had no evidence for their association of partners with God; they followed their desires without knowledge, so no one can guide those whom God has led astray, and they will have no helpers against punishment. The commentators explain "whom God has led astray" as those whom God has decreed to be misguided. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy keep to this literal sense. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, reads the leading astray as God forsaking the person and withholding His grace, grounding this in the Mu'tazili view that God does not create evil; he notes that the Sunni position, that God creates evil as He creates good, keeps the verse on its apparent meaning. Al-Razi holds that the polytheists' straying happened by God's will. The turn introduced by "bal" returns to what precedes: they had neither proof nor excuse. The commentators define desire (hawa) as what the soul inclines towards, and several note that following it without knowledge is worse than following it knowingly, since a learned person may be restrained by his knowledge. As for the next verse, which orders the Prophet to set his face toward the religion as a pure believer, most read it as an obligation to remain upon the fitra of God, meaning monotheism or Islam, citing the hadith that every child is born upon the fitra. Others take it as the covenant God made with the offspring of Adam, and some read "no change in God's creation" as a prohibition against altering the religion, while Ikrima took it as a prohibition against castrating animals.

The verse commands the Prophet ﷺ and those who follow him to turn their faces to the upright religion, hanif, meaning leaning away from false creeds toward pure Islam. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur, take the "fitra of God" to mean the religion in which God created people, that is Islam and monotheism, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim understand it as the innate disposition by which a person recognises the Creator and accepts the truth.

The phrase "no altering of God's creation" is read by Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd as meaning there is no altering of God's religion. Ikrima, Umar and, in one report, Ibn Abbas, take it to forbid castrating animals. Some read it as a prohibition expressed in the form of a statement.

The commentators agree that people are naturally inclined to recognise the truth, and several cite the hadith that every child is born upon the fitra and that his parents make him a Jew or a Christian. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani note, however, that this innate faith does not make the child a Muslim for the purposes of worldly rulings. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that parents cause the change without altering the original nature, while al-Zamakhshari stresses that humans are created apt for monotheism and turn from it only under the influence of devils.

The "upright religion" is for most scholars Islam or straight monotheism, though Ibn Abbas links it to sound judgement. As for the "sects" mentioned, Ibn Kathir sees them as those who divided their religion, and he counts innovators among them, as al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya also do, while others such as al-Zamakhshari identify them with deviants who separated from Islam.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ and the believers who follow him to set their faces and purpose toward the upright religion, turning away from every corrupted creed, to return to God in repentance and obedience, to fear Him, to establish prayer, and not to be among the polytheists. The commentators agree that the religion meant is Islam and monotheism. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain the fitra of God as Islam and monotheism, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as the natural disposition of human beings to accept the truth, and others as the covenant taken from the children of Adam. On the words 'no change in the creation of God', Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it to mean no change in the religion of God, 'Ikrima and al-Bukhari take it as a prohibition against castrating male animals, and others as a statement that the original nature does not change from the Creator's side.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain 'munibin' as turning back to God and facing Him, and al-Mawardi notes that the root can also mean cutting oneself off for God. According to Qatada and Mu'ammar, those who divided their religion are Jews and Christians, while according to Abu Hurayra, 'A'isha and Abu Umama they are the people of innovation and desire within this community. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the polytheists in the verse are the People of the Book or the people of the qibla depending on the interpretation. All agree that each faction rejoices in what it has. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur draw from the passage a warning to Muslims against division and partisan zeal.

This passage of Surat al-Rum commands the Prophet ﷺ and the believers to turn their faces toward the upright religion, which is Islam, turning away from all other paths, and to adhere to the fitra, the natural disposition on which God created people. Commentators explain the fitra either as the innate capacity to recognize and worship God alone, or as Islam itself. The phrase 'there is no alteration in the creation of God' is understood by most as a prohibition against changing this nature, or as an affirmation that God's religion does not change. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima took it to mean a prohibition against castrating animals. The next verse calls for turning back to God in repentance, fearing Him, establishing prayer, and not being among the polytheists who divided their religion and became sects. Qatada, Ma'mar and Ibn Zayd identify these people as Jews and Christians; Abu Hurayra, 'A'isha and Abu Umama say they are the people of innovation and desires within this community. Commentators accept both readings. The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, 'faraqu', means that they abandoned their religion. According to Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir, the 'sects' are groups each following the leader who misguided them, and 'each party rejoices in what it has' means they are pleased with their beliefs, thinking them to be true. Al-Razi distinguishes blameworthy joy in worldly possessions from the joy of the sincere soul in what is with God. The overall meaning is that unity upon the natural religion is obligatory, and that division and partisan attachment to one's own group resemble the conduct of the polytheists.

This verse describes how people behave in hardship and in ease. The commentators agree that when people are struck by harm, such as drought, illness or distress, they turn to God alone in humble supplication. When God relieves them and grants mercy, meaning rain, health or prosperity, a group among them returns to associating others with Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi apply this to the idolaters of Quraysh and other polytheists, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it more broadly as a warning against anyone who credits his deliverance to something other than God. They explain that the word 'a group' refers to the associators alone, since believers are not included. There is disagreement over the meaning of 'harm' and 'mercy': some take them to be drought and rain, others illness and well-being. On the phrase 'so that they may deny what We have given them', most read the particle as expressing consequence or purpose, while some take the following 'enjoy yourselves' as a command of threat, a reading attributed to Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Mas'ud. For 'an authority', Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean proof, while Qatada and al-Rabi' take it to mean a revealed book. The overall sense is a denial that any evidence supports polytheism. The commentators also clarify that the blameworthy despair is giving up on God's mercy, and the blameworthy joy is that of arrogance which does not give thanks.

This passage in Surat al-Rum describes people who, struck by a hardship such as drought or distress, turn to God alone and return to Him, but who, as soon as mercy reaches them, revert to associating others with God. The commentators explain that the particle in « li-yakfurū » (so that they may deny) expresses a consequence rather than a purpose: what they do ends in ingratitude for the blessing received. The command « fa-tamatta'ū fa-sawfa ta'lamūn » (enjoy yourselves, then you will soon know) is, for most, a threat. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi agree that the reference is to the idolaters of Mecca, and understand mercy as abundance and well-being and harm as drought and adversity. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi read the imperative as a threat, while al-Qurtubi allows that the lam may be an imperative lam carrying the sense of menace. Some early readers recited « fa-sawfa yaʿlamūn » in the third person, and Ibn Mas'ud read « wa-li-yatamatta'ū ».

Regarding « am anzalna 'alayhim sultānan » (or have We sent down on them an authority?), al-Tabari takes it as a book that speaks of their associating others with God. Al-Mawardi records several senses: a book according to ad-Dahhak, an excuse according to Qatada, a proof according to as-Suddi and 'Ata'. The overall meaning is a rhetorical denial: God has sent down no evidence to justify their polytheism.

The commentators also agree on the nature of the censure: joy that leads to arrogance is condemned, as is despair in the face of trial. Ibn Kathir sees here a general rule about humankind, except for those whom God protects, and cites the hadith about the believer for whom every outcome is good. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur stress the wrongfulness of returning to idolatry once relief has come.

This passage describes people who, struck by hardship such as drought or illness, turn to God alone in repentance, but once He relieves them, a group of them returns to associating others with Him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the blessing as something that drives them to deny God's favour, with Ibn Kathir taking the lam as one of consequence and al-Tabari as one of warning. The word sultan is understood by most commentators as proof or a revealed book, and the question is one of denial: God has sent no evidence to justify their associating. Qatadah and Ibn Abbas render it as a plea or excuse, and al-Mawardi lists several meanings including ruler. Al-Razi notes that speech is a metaphor here, since a claim without proof is as if it had no speech. Ibn Juzayy sees it simply as the lack of any proof. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di add that humans rejoice arrogantly when blessed and despair when tried, whereas the believer gives thanks in ease and hopes in hardship. Ibn Sa'di also presents the expansion and restriction of provision as a sign for believers. The commentators agree that association has no revealed basis and springs from desire and ignorance.

This verse describes how people behave when circumstances change. When God grants people a blessing such as rain, prosperity or good health, they rejoice in an arrogant and boastful way rather than with gratitude. When a misfortune strikes them, such as drought, sickness or poverty, which the commentators link to their own sins, they fall into despair. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir agree that the mercy is a blessing such as rain, ease or health, and that the evil is a trial such as famine, hardship or illness. Most see the verse as describing unbelievers, or people generally when they are comfortable or in trouble. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, explain qunut as losing hope of relief and mercy, while al-Hasan al-Basri understands it as neglecting God's obligations when life is easy. On the reading, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read the verb with a kasra, while most readers use a fatha, both being accepted forms. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi note that the verse names the cause of the misfortune but not that of the blessing, which they take to show God's justice in punishment and grace in giving. Al-Razi separates the joy that stops at the blessing itself, which he condemns, from joy that turns to the Giver, which he approves, and says the believer thanks God in ease and hopes in God in hardship, a view Ibn Sa'di also expresses. The verse closes by reminding the reader that God expands and restricts provision as He wills, a sign for believers.

This verse affirms that Allah alone expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it for whom He wills, and that there are clear signs in this for believers. The commentators read it as a rebuke against people who rejoice arrogantly when blessed and despair of relief when afflicted, though they should know that all matters rest with God. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that mercy means plenty, health and ease, that evil means drought and hardship, and that qunut is despair of God's mercy, whereas the believer gives thanks in ease and hopes in God in adversity. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi see the expansion and restriction as a divine test. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi point out that despairing after acknowledging that God both gives and withholds is inconsistent. The next verse, which orders that the near relative, the needy and the traveller be given their due, has produced differing views on the riba it mentions. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi mostly report that it means a gift given in expectation of a greater return, which carries neither reward nor sin, while al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i take it to be a gift made to obtain service or to increase wealth, and al-Dahhak restricts it to the Prophet ﷺ. All agree that zakat is charity given for God's pleasure, whose reward is multiplied.

This verse tells the believer to give the near relative his due, and likewise the poor man and the traveller in need, and it declares that this is better for those who seek the Face of God, who are the prosperous. The commentators explain that the near relative is owed kinship duties, through wealth, kindness and good words; that the poor man should be given enough to meet his needs; and that the traveller should be sheltered and helped on his journey. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the address is to the Prophet, with his community following him, and that sincere intention is what makes the giving beneficial to the giver. Al-Hasan holds that this due means helping in ease and speaking kindly in hardship. On who the relatives are, Ibn Abbas and others mean the giver's own kin, while al-Suddi identifies them as the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, who receive their share of spoils and fay. Mujahid says the duty of kinship is an obligation, and that charity is not accepted from someone whose needy relative is left unhelped. The Shafi'is restrict the duty of maintenance to parents and children, while Abu Hanifa cites the verse for maintaining needy unemployable kin. Some consider the verse abrogated by the inheritance verses, while others say its ruling stands. Finally, the Face of God means seeking His pleasure, and whoever acts for show gains no reward.

This verse contrasts two kinds of giving. What is given in order to grow one's wealth at the expense of others, such as usury or a gift hoped to be returned with more, does not increase in God's sight and earns no reward for its giver. Charity given seeking God's face is what God multiplies for those who give it. Most commentators understand the riba here as a gift one makes hoping for more in return. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Qatada explain it as a present given expecting a better one back, which is permitted but carries no reward; al-Dahhak adds that this was specifically forbidden to the Prophet, citing the verse 'do not give expecting to receive more'. Al-Sha'bi understands it as what is paid to someone who serves a man on a journey or at work, and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i as what is given to a relative to increase his wealth. Al-Suddi says the verse was revealed about the forbidden usury practised by the tribe of Thaqif. For the zakat, nearly all take it as charity given for God's face. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the shift to the third person in 'those are the multipliers' is a mark of honour. Al-Razi clarifies that the multiplication concerns the reward, not the quantity given. Al-Qurtubi notes the scholarly disagreement over gifts made in expectation of a return. The readings 'liyarbu' and 'litarbu' are discussed, and al-Tabari considers both close in meaning.

This verse states that God alone created people, then provided for them, then causes them to die, and then will bring them back to life, and that none of the associates the polytheists worship does any of these things. Commentators read it as a rebuke to the idolaters and as a demonstration of their idols' powerlessness. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the argument rests on what the pagans themselves acknowledge, namely creation and provision. Ibn Kathir adds that God brings a person out of the mother's womb with no knowledge, hearing or sight, and then grants everything he needs. They agree that the question is rhetorical and that the expected answer is no.

The commentators also agree that the word "then" marks sequence, and that repeating the particle "min" strengthens the negation. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss the grammar of the sentence, the role of the demonstrative "dhalikum" in linking the clause to its subject, and the possible readings. These are grammatical points that do not produce doctrinal disagreement.

The main difference concerns death and life. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand the final giving of life as the resurrection on the Day of Judgment. Ibn 'Uthaymin distinguishes death, which is the complete separation of soul and body, from the life in the grave that precedes resurrection. Al-Shawkani and al-Qasimi limit themselves to the denial of associates without developing this point. Al-Razi explicitly links the verse to the twofold proof of resurrection and divine oneness. Al-Sha'rawi distinguishes killing from causing death, a distinction the other commentators do not draw.

Finally, the commentators agree that the closing phrase, "Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him," declares God free of any partner. There is no notable disagreement on this point.

This verse says that corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned, and that God makes them taste some of what they have done so that they may return. The commentators understood "land" and "sea" in closely related ways. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Mujahid take land to mean the wastelands and sea to mean the towns and villages beside flowing water, and 'Ikrima notes that the Arabs call cities seas. Al-Tabari holds that the word covers any body of water, sweet or salt, and therefore includes the settlements along rivers and seas. Qatada distinguishes the desert dwellers from the people of towns and villages. Al-Hasan says land and sea are the familiar realities, and that corruption appears in them through the loss of blessings, the coming of calamities, the rise of strife and the domination of an enemy.

Opinions differ on the nature of this corruption. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Mujahid cite the killing of Abel by Cain on land and a ruler seizing every ship by force at sea. Others, such as 'Ata' and Ibn Abi Najih, speak of drought, scarce rain, a decline in pearls and the disappearance of sea creatures. Al-Suddi identifies it with polytheism, the gravest corruption, while Abu al-'Aliya links it to disobedience in general. The scholars agree that the punishment is only a part of what is deserved, the rest being reserved for the Hereafter, and that the lam in "to make them taste" expresses purpose or consequence. Ibn al-Qayyim ties these afflictions to the loss of blessings in water, air, crops and fruit.

The passage then calls people to travel through the earth and see the fate of earlier peoples, most of whom were associators. Commentators disagreed on what this implies: some hold that all of them perished, others that most were punished, and others that the verse warns against polytheism and calls to faith.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to tell the Quraysh to travel through the land and observe the fate of earlier peoples, so as to learn the outcome of those who rejected the messengers. The commentators agree that this outcome was destruction and ruin, and that polytheism prevailed among those peoples. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take the address to be to the Quraysh, and read the verse as an invitation to reflect on the now-empty dwellings of the destroyed. They differ on the force of the clause 'most of whom were polytheists'. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di take polytheism to be the cause of the destruction, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi hold that polytheism alone was not the cause and that other sins also led to it. Al-Razi argues that the punishment did not spare non-polytheists, such as children and the insane, whereas Ibn 'Ashur sees the clause as giving the reason for the warning that precedes it. On the following verses, the commentators agree that the upright religion is Islam, that the day that cannot be turned back is the Day of Resurrection, and that on that day people will separate into two groups, one for Paradise and one for the Blaze. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that 'corruption on land and sea' admits several readings, including drought, loss of blessing, sins, Qabil's killing of his brother and the seizure of ships, and none of them settles the matter.

The verse commands the Prophet to set his face toward the upright religion, meaning Islam without any crookedness, before the Day of Resurrection comes, a day that no one can turn back, when people will separate into two groups, one in Paradise and one in the Blaze. Qatada identifies the upright religion with Islam, as-Suddi with monotheism, and Ibn 'Isa reads it as a call to steadfastness until the believer reaches Paradise. Az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi describe it as a religion of perfect straightness. The commentators agree that the verb rendered as scatter means to separate, and that the separation is between Paradise and Hell; Ibn 'Abbas and others cite a line of poetry to illustrate the sense. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the address an implicit warning to the polytheists, and suggests the day mentioned may be the day of Badr or the gathering.

The verse links faith to deeds, as al-Razi, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain: whoever disbelieves bears the weight of his disbelief, and whoever does righteous deeds prepares a resting place for himself, a phrase Mujahid applies to the grave. Ibn Kathir notes that the reward is a grace from God that exceeds the deeds, and that God does not love the disbelievers. Al-Razi explains the fronting of the prepositional phrases by saying that the harm of disbelief falls only on the disbeliever, while the benefit of faith and good works returns to the believer alone.

The corruption mentioned in the preceding verses is also understood in several ways: Ibn al-Jawzi reports views that it means the loss of blessing, sin, polytheism or drought, while Mujahid takes it as Cain's killing of Abel and the seizure of ships by force. Ibn Kathir explains that such partial punishment is meant to bring people back to repentance.

The commentators explain that the verse means that whoever disbelieves bears alone the burden of his disbelief, and whoever does righteous deeds is preparing a resting place for himself. Mujahid understands this as making the beds in the graves, while Yahya ibn Salam takes it as preparation in this world through the Qur'an and in the Hereafter through good deeds. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi read it as preparing dwellings in Paradise. The commentators agree that the harm of disbelief falls only on the disbeliever and that the reward of faith and good works returns to the one who does them. Al-Zamakhshari reads the fronting of the prepositional phrases as restricting the effect to the doer, whereas Ibn 'Ashur and Abu Hayyan see it as emphasis or as a concern for rhyme rather than exclusivity. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya link the phrase "that He may reward" to the verb of preparing, while Ibn Kathir understands the bounty as a multiplication of reward beyond what deeds merit.
