Several scholars note that the verse contrasts the disbeliever with the doer of good rather than with the believer, which Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi explain as a way of honouring faith and urging believers not to rely on belief alone.

This verse states that God rewards those who believe and do righteous deeds out of His bounty, meaning a favour that exceeds what their deeds deserve, and that He does not love the disbelievers. Most commentators hold that the primary aim is the reward of the believers, and that the denial of God's love signifies His displeasure and the punishment that follows. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Baghawi, explains that God rewards them more than the worth of their deeds, and Ibn Kathir adds that a good deed may be multiplied up to seven hundred times and beyond. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read the closing phrase as a restatement by inversion, establishing that believers are loved by God and disbelievers are denied His favour. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi stress that reward is pure grace and not something owed to God. Most commentators link the phrase 'so that' to what precedes it, either to 'they prepare' or to 'they will be divided', meaning that they separate into two groups, one in Paradise and one in the Blaze, as Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report. The meaning of 'they prepare' is understood in different ways: Mujahid takes it as arranging the resting places in the graves, al-Zamakhshari as preparing a dwelling in Paradise, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy as a metaphor drawn from spreading a bed. Al-Razi notes that the verse mentions the disbeliever first when speaking of human responsibility, and the believer first when speaking of divine reward.

In this verse God shows that among His signs, which reveal His power and mercy, is that He sends winds that bring good news of rain. Through them He lets His servants taste His mercy, which is the rain that gives life to the lands and people, makes ships sail on the sea by His command, and allows people to seek His bounty through trade, so that they may be grateful. Most commentators understand the mercy as rain: Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak say the winds bring the glad tidings of rain, and al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir describe the mercy as rain and fertility. Al-Mawardi adds the pleasant coolness of the air, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur mention the fertilising of trees, the winnowing of grain and the clearing of foul air. Opinions differ on the winds themselves. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud say that the south, north and east winds are winds of mercy and the west wind is a wind of punishment, relying on a report of the Prophet seeking refuge from a harmful wind. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that the variety of winds, and the use of the plural for mercy and the singular for punishment, carries wisdom. Al-Razi observes that the verse mentions improving the air first, then rain, then sailing. Al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan note that the singular reading fits the sense of a kind. Regarding the end of the passage, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya state that God made the victory of believers a right He imposed on Himself, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn identify the 'clear proofs' as the miracles of the prophets. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a consolation for the Prophet.

This verse states that God sent messengers before the Prophet ﷺ to their peoples, who came to them with clear proofs; the wrongdoers among them denied them, and God punished them, while it was a binding truth that He would give victory to the believers. Most commentators, beginning with al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, read it as a consolation to the Prophet regarding what his fellow messengers suffered, and as a warning to his own people that they would meet a similar fate. Al-Tabari understands the 'clear proofs' as evident arguments for the messengers' truthfulness, while al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and others take them to be signs and miracles. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir interpret the punishment as destruction in this world. The commentators agree that the victory of the believers means their deliverance with the messengers from punishment, as al-Hasan al-Basri said. Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take 'haqqan' as the predicate of 'kana' and 'victory of the believers' as its subject, stressing the honour given to believers. Some readers pause at 'haqqan', making the punishment itself just; Ibn Atiyya and al-Kawashi consider this weak. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Shawkani, cite the hadith of Abu al-Darda' about defending a Muslim brother's honour, though Ibn Kathir and others note its weak chain. Ibn Ashur sees an allusion to Noah's flood and a warning to Quraysh. Ibn Sa'di concludes that this support is a duty God imposed on Himself, even if it may be delayed.

The commentators explain that God sends the winds that stir up the clouds and spreads them across the sky as He wills, sometimes as one continuous mass and sometimes in scattered pieces, so that rain comes forth from between them. When He sends it to whomever He wills among His servants, they rejoice. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take wadq to mean rain, while al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani report that some said it means lightning, though they consider rain the stronger view. All agree that mublisin means despairing. The repetition of 'min qablihi' has several readings: al-Akhfash and most grammarians treat it as emphasis, Qutrub assigns the two occurrences to the descent and to the rain, Ibn 'Atiyya sees in it how quickly hearts move from despair to joy, and al-Zamakhshari sees the length of the wait, which makes the joy match the distress. Al-Razi prefers that it refers to the sending of the winds, since a breeze alone does not yet show whether rain is coming. The reading 'kisfan' with or without the vowel changes little in meaning, according to Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi. The passage then turns to the revival of the earth by rain as proof of the resurrection. Ibn Kathir adds that a scorching wind that withers the crops becomes a punishment, and people respond with ingratitude, while al-Mawardi reports that the pronoun in 'fa-ra'awhu' refers to the plants according to Ibn 'Abbas and Abu 'Ubayda, and to the clouds according to others.

The commentators explain that God sends the winds that stir up the clouds and spread them across the sky as He wills, then breaks them into scattered pieces, and rain comes out from within them. Those He reaches with this rain rejoice, having been despairing and downcast before it fell. Most agree that 'mublisun' means despairing and dejected at the withholding of rain, and that its arrival after such despair is felt all the more deeply. On the repetition of 'min qablihi', opinions differ. Al-Akhfash and most grammarians take it as emphasis, which al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya use to show how long the people had gone without rain and how firmly their despair had set. Qutrub reads the first 'before' as relating to the sending down and the second to the rain itself. Others take the pronoun to refer to the sight of the clouds, to the sending of the winds, or to the joy itself, a view al-Nahhas favours.

The exegetes then link the verse to what follows. The earth revived after its death becomes a visible proof that God can bring the dead back to life, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state. Al-Tabari notes that the two readings, 'athar' and 'athar', come to nearly the same meaning. Ibn Kathir understands 'mercy' as the rain, while al-Shawkani notes it may denote God's mercy itself.

In short, rain is a blessing that gladdens hearts after despair, and what the eye sees of the revived land is evidence that resurrection is possible, for God is powerful over all things.

This verse calls the listener to look at the traces of Allah's mercy in the rain: the dead earth comes back to life and brings forth plants after its dryness. The commentators say that whoever has the power to do this also has the power to bring the dead back to life, since He is powerful over all things. The verse follows the description of the winds stirring the clouds and the rain falling, and it recalls that people were despairing before the downpour and then rejoiced. On the repetition of "before it" (min qablihi), al-Akhfash and most grammarians see it as emphasis, a view also taken by az-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi. Qutrub holds that the pronoun refers back to the rain, while others take it as a separate statement, with the pronoun referring to the moment of rejoicing or to an earlier period of drought, a view Ibn Kathir preferred, counting several seasons of failed rain. On the readings "athar" in the singular and "athar" in the plural, Ibn 'Atiyya explains the plural as the variety of plants and fruits, whereas Ibn Kathir and others take mercy to mean the rain itself. Most exegetes make Allah the subject of "yuhyi", though some attribute the action to the rain's effect. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that this is reasoning from the visible to the unseen, that is, the resurrection. Al-Razi observes that the noun form "muhyi" expresses the lasting nature of the attribute. All agree on the core lesson: God's power and mercy are shown in the life the rain restores to the earth.

This verse describes how people rejoice in rain and the fertility of the land, yet quickly turn to ingratitude when a wind destroys their crops. The commentators generally understand the pronoun in «fa-ra'awhu» as referring to the plants, or to the trace of mercy, meaning the green crops that turned yellow under a destructive wind, as Ibn Abbas, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that the wind may be the dabur, and that it may be hot or cold, while others simply call it harmful. Some hold that the pronoun refers to the clouds, since yellowed clouds do not bring rain, and others that it refers to the wind; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider these two views weak. As for «zallu», most explain it as «they became» or «they will surely», and al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya note that the past tense stands for the future because the conditional answer must be in the future. On the meaning of «yakfurun», al-Tabari, Muqatil and Ibn Kathir take it as ingratitude for the earlier blessing, while al-Mawardi allows the sense of doubt or blame. The following verses tell the Prophet that he cannot make the dead hear, nor the deaf who turn their backs hear his call, nor lead the blind out of their error, and that he makes only those who believe in God's signs hear and submit. Most read this as an image for the disbelievers, and al-Razi notes that a warning benefits only the one who accepts it.

This verse, within a passage about rain and about people's swings between despair and joy, consoles the Prophet ﷺ over the refusal of his people. The commentators explain its plain meaning: just as you cannot make the dead hear your words so that they understand them, nor make the deaf hear your call when they turn their backs, so you cannot guide those whose hearing and hearts God has sealed. Qatada reads the verse as an image for the disbelievers, who hear without benefiting, as the dead and the turning-away deaf do not hear. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that guidance belongs to God alone, and that the words "you make hear only those who believe in Our signs, and they submit" refer to the useful hearing of believers who reflect on the Book and submit to it. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that guiding them is neither within your power nor your duty. Al-Mawardi gives two readings of the dead: unbelievers who died in disbelief, or a figurative image for the disbelievers. Some scholars note that a deaf person facing the speaker may grasp meaning from signs, while one who turns away understands nothing, which explains why the turning away is mentioned. On whether the dead hear, opinions differ: Aisha cited the verse to deny that the dead of Badr heard the Prophet, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that the dead hear in general and that the verse concerns beneficial hearing. Al-Alusi concludes that they hear to some degree, by God's will.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the image of the crop turned yellow by the wind, and states that disbelievers who turn away from God in hardship are not reached by the message. They are likened to the dead who cannot hear, to the deaf who turn their backs, and to the blind who have lost their way. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur take these images to refer to disbelievers whom God has deprived of hearing and of sight in the heart, so the Prophet cannot guide them. Only the one who believes in God's signs and submits to him truly hears, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya add that mentioning the deaf who turn away makes the impossibility of hearing stronger. Al-Baydawi explains that the blind are so called because their hearts are blind. Regarding the dead, al-Mawardi reports two views: that of Yahya ibn Sallam, who sees them as disbelievers who died in unbelief, and the reading that treats the image as a parable. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi develop the question of whether the dead can hear, citing the Badr incident and 'A'isha's objection. Ibn Kathir judges Ibn 'Umar's version the most authentic, while al-Alusi lists several opinions without deciding. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the sense is useful hearing. Ibn 'Ashur distinguishes three groups of disbelievers, each compared to one of these images. Al-Biqa'i and al-Alusi understand the one who hears as the believer who reflects and is ready for faith, and they read the verse as a consolation for the Prophet facing their refusal.

This verse describes the stages of human life: weakness at the start, strength in youth, and then weakness again in old age marked by grey hair. Dhe commentators agree that God created man from a weak fluid or in childhood weakness, granted him strength in youth, and then returned him to weakness and old age, by His knowledge and power. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read the first weakness as the drop of fluid, the strength as youth, and the final weakness as decrepitude. Ibn Kathir reports the hadith transmitted through Ibn Umar, who recited with a fatha and was corrected by the Prophet to a damma. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the damma is the stronger reading, and that the fatha is the dialect of Tamim while the damma belongs to Quraysh. Some linguists, as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan record, distinguish the damma for bodily weakness from the fatha for weakness of mind, while others reject this. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi argue that the sequence of these states is clear proof of the Creator's knowledge and power. Al-Mawardi and Qatada see grey hair as a warning of death. In the following verses, the sinners swear they stayed only an hour; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take this as a lie, as they lied in the world, while Ibn 'Atiyya suggests they belittled their worldly life compared to the Hereafter, and Abu Hayyan mentions forgetfulness or falsehood.

This verse describes how, on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they tarried only a short while, whether in the life of this world or in their graves. The commentators explain that they regard their stay as very brief, either out of terror at what they see or because it appears short next to what awaits them. Most agree that the criminals are the polytheists and disbelievers, and that their oath is a lie, just as they lied in this world. Ibn Kathir sees the oath as an attempt to escape the proof, since they were not given time to be warned. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the word "yu'fakun" means being turned away from the truth, so they were turned from it in this life just as they are turned in the next.

Opinions differ about the period meant. Qatada, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to be the worldly life, while Muqatil and al-Kalbi also take it to be the stay in the graves, and Yahya ibn Salam places it between death and resurrection. Al-Qurtubi notes that a hadith about forty between the two blasts does not settle the matter and does not deny the punishment of the grave. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir then connect the following verse to the learned believers, who answer that their stay was written in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the word "sa'a" here is the Hour of Resurrection itself, a name given to it because it arrives suddenly. They draw no conclusion that departs from this reading of the verse.

This verse reports that those given knowledge and faith, identified by most commentators as angels, prophets and believers, answer the idolaters who swore they had remained only an hour, whether in worldly life or in their graves. They tell them that they remained in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection, and that this is the Day of Resurrection they used to deny, but that they did not know it would come. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the Book refers to what God decreed in His prior knowledge. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi add that it may mean the Preserved Tablet, the divine judgment, or the Quran itself. Qatada, Muqatil and al-Suddi held that there is an inversion of word order, so that the knowledgeable ones are those who know the Book, a reading which Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan found too strained for the structure of the text.

The commentators agree that the fa in fa-hadha yawmu al-ba'th answers an implied condition, meaning: if you deny resurrection, then this is its day. They see the words as a rebuke that exposes the error of the deniers. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that the believers reply with the same proof the deniers rejected in the world. Al-Razi links the verses to the difference between the guilty, who find the delay short, and the believers, who find it long.

The next verse, the commentators agree, states that the wrongdoers will gain nothing from their excuses on that day, and that they will not be asked to make amends by returning to right conduct.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoers, meaning those who wronged themselves through disbelief and polytheism, will not benefit from their excuses, and they will not be asked to restore God's favour through repentance and obedience as they were in this world. The commentators explain that the excuse is the justification by which one tries to ward off punishment, and that istiʿtab means to seek to be pleased, that is, to return to what satisfies God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAtiyya report that the disbelievers will swear they stayed in the world only an hour, and that the learned believers will answer that they remained in the Book of God until the Day of Resurrection, but that they did not know it. Al-Zamakhshari reads the fa' in the phrase 'this is the Day of Resurrection' as answering an implied condition: if you deny resurrection, then this is its day. On the meaning of istiʿtab, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that they will not be told to make amends, al-Naqqash understands that they will not be reproached for their sins, and Yahya ibn Salam sees it as a request to return to the world to believe. As for who received knowledge, al-Kalbi identifies them as the angels, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj as the believers, and others as the People of the Book. Readers differ between the yā' and the tā' in the verb, without changing the overall meaning that the excuse will be of no avail that day.

This verse states that God has explained to people, in the Quran, every kind of striking parable and description, to establish the proof against them and to draw them to monotheism and the truth of the messengers. It adds that if the disbelievers were brought any sign, they would say to the Prophet and the believers that they are upholders of falsehood. The commentators agree that the disbelievers are stubborn deniers, and that their obstinacy and hardness of heart is the cause of their rejection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the sign may be a miracle such as Moses' staff or the splitting of the sea, or a verse of the Quran itself, and that they would reject it whatever it was, calling it sorcery. As for the phrase 'Thus God seals the hearts of those who do not know', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a sealing that prevents them from understanding the verses. Al-Zamakhshari, however, takes the seal to mean the withholding of the favours that open the heart to truth, a reading he ties to Mu'tazili doctrine, and he himself notes that the Sunni position holds God creates this sealing as He creates good. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi speak of a compound ignorance that blocks the perception of truth. The verse ends with the command to the Prophet to be patient, since God's promise is true, and not to be swayed by those who do not believe in resurrection. Al-Tabari recounts in this context the report of a Kharijite who called out to Ali during the dawn prayer and was answered with this same verse. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Ashur also mention an opinion that the verse was abrogated, without a firm conclusion.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the description of how the disbelievers react to the signs: God states that their rejection of every sign results from a seal placed upon their hearts, so that they neither accept the truth nor understand the Quranic verses recited to them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi specify that these are the hearts of the ignorant, who do not seek knowledge and cling to superstitions they have adopted. Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and Ibn Kathir add that compound ignorance blocks the perception of truth and leads a person to call the one who speaks truth a liar. Al-Zamakhshari reads the sealing as God withholding the favours that open the heart to truth, and he notes that according to the Sunni position God creates this sealing, so the verse is taken literally, as al-Alusi also records. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a state that makes the heart unable to grasp religious matters, and he identifies those who do not know with the disbelievers themselves. Al-Razi observes that whoever does not know now has been sealed earlier. Most agree that the verse consoles the Prophet, and the following verse commands patience because God's promise is true and those without certainty must not unsettle him. Al-Sa'di and al-Biqa'i clarify that the knowledge they lack is the beneficial knowledge that guides to truth. Some report an episode in which a Kharijite addressed Ali during prayer, but the commentators draw no legal ruling from it.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to be patient with his opponents, because God's promise is true, and it forbids him to be moved by those who lack certainty. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the promise as the victory of the Prophet and the establishment of his followers on earth, while al-Mawardi also mentions retribution against enemies, and al-Sam'ani takes it to mean the Resurrection. The word translated as being moved is read by most commentators as a call not to hasten, not to be provoked, or not to be drawn into error, and the people without certainty are generally identified as those who deny resurrection and judgement. Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi describe them as doubters who are astray, while Abu Hayyan says they do not believe the promised victory. Several scholars, including al-Tha'alibi, report that during the dawn prayer a Kharijite addressed Ali with a threatening verse, and Ali answered him with this verse within the prayer. Zamakhshari notes a variant reading, yastahiqqanaka, and a lighter pronunciation of the final nun attributed to Ya'qub. Ibn al-Qayyim links steadfastness to patience and certainty, while al-Shinqiti explains that although the address is to the Prophet, its purpose is to instruct his community, since he is protected from disbelief.
